questions.stem: The Yellow River (Huang He) gets its name from:
options: the gold dust found in its riverbed
the Yellow Emperor, who dug its course
the yellow loess silt that it carries
the yellow robes worn by the emperors
questions.explanation: The river picks up huge amounts of fine yellow loess soil from the plateau it crosses, and where it drops this silt the land is fertile and easy to farm, which made its valley a cradle of early Chinese civilisation. The Yangtze, further south, became a major rice-growing region. Yellow later became the imperial colour, but the river's name comes from its silt.

questions.stem: Why was the Yellow River also called 'China's Sorrow'?
options: It froze solid every winter and cut off all of the river trade
Its water was too salty to be used for irrigating crops
Invading armies used it to sail straight to the capital
Its frequent floods and changes of course killed many people
questions.explanation: Silt builds up in the riverbed, raising it above the surrounding plain, so when the banks break the river can flood vast areas and even shift its course. Controlling floods was one of the main duties expected of rulers, which is why the legend of Yu the Great taming the floods mattered so much.

questions.stem: Why are Shang dynasty oracle bones important evidence for historians?
options: They were the first coins ever used for trade in China
They show maps of the Shang cities and the roads between
They list the laws that every Shang family had to obey
They carry the earliest known form of Chinese writing
questions.explanation: Shang kings had questions carved on ox bones and turtle shells, which were heated until they cracked; diviners read the cracks as answers from ancestors and gods about harvests, war, weather and illness. The inscriptions are the earliest substantial Chinese writing and confirmed that the Shang, once known only from later histories, really existed. The Shang were also skilled bronze-casters.

questions.stem: According to the Mandate of Heaven, a ruler's right to rule:
options: came from Heaven, and could be lost if he ruled badly
passed automatically to his eldest son for all time
depended on winning a vote of the leading officials
belonged only to the descendants of the sage Confucius
questions.explanation: The Zhou used the Mandate of Heaven to justify overthrowing the Shang around 1046 BCE, claiming the last Shang king had lost Heaven's support through cruelty. The idea meant a dynasty ruled only while it governed well. Confucius lived centuries later and never founded a ruling family.

questions.stem: Under the idea of the Mandate of Heaven, how might people interpret a period of floods, famine and peasant revolts?
options: As a sign the dynasty had lost Heaven's support and could be replaced
As proof that the emperor needed to build a longer Great Wall
As a punishment because ordinary people had stopped following the Dao
As a test the emperor had to pass before his son could inherit
questions.explanation: Disasters and rebellions were read as signs that Heaven was withdrawing its approval from the ruler, and a rebel leader could claim that his victory showed the Mandate had passed to him. A successful rebellion therefore became its own proof. This helps explain the pattern of rise, decline and replacement of dynasties in Chinese history.

questions.stem: The Art of War, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu and written in an age of constant warfare, advises that:
options: the greatest victory is to defeat the enemy without fighting
a general should always attack the strongest part of the enemy
soldiers must never retreat, whatever the cost in lives
rulers should choose their generals by holding an examination
questions.explanation: The book stresses planning, deception, knowing yourself and your enemy and avoiding costly battles, famously saying that defeating an enemy without fighting is the highest skill. It advises attacking weakness rather than strength. It comes from around the Warring States period (475–221 BCE), when huge infantry armies, crossbows and chariots made war deadly and constant.

questions.stem: In Confucian teaching, what does filial piety mean?
options: Living simply and in harmony with the natural world
Respect, obedience and care for parents and ancestors
Loyalty to the gods above any loyalty to one's family
Strict obedience to written laws and their punishments
questions.explanation: Confucius taught that society would be orderly if people behaved properly in their relationships, starting at home: children owed parents respect and care, including honouring ancestors after death. Strict laws and punishments were the approach of Legalism, and living simply in harmony with nature is the Daoist ideal.

questions.stem: The five relationships of Confucian thought are ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and:
options: friend and friend
teacher and student
master and slave
emperor and Heaven
questions.explanation: Four of the five relationships are unequal, with the senior partner owing kindness and the junior owing respect and obedience; only friendship is between equals. Teachers were greatly respected in Confucian culture, but teacher and student is not one of the five. The relationships guided behaviour in families and in government alike.

questions.stem: Confucius described the ideal person as a junzi. What was a junzi?
options: A ruler who controls the strongest army among all the states
A hermit who lives apart from society high in the mountains
A merchant who grows rich by trading goods along the rivers
A person of virtue who acts with respect, honesty and learning
questions.explanation: Junzi is often translated as 'gentleman' or 'exemplary person': for Confucius it meant someone who became noble through moral character and study rather than through birth. A ruler was meant to lead by such example rather than by force. A hermit withdrawing from society fits Daoist ideals better, and merchants had low status in Confucian thinking.

questions.stem: Daoism, linked to the thinker Laozi, teaches that people should:
options: carry out rituals and their duties to family and ruler
seek wealth and power in order to bring order to the state
live simply and in harmony with the natural way, the Dao
obey harsh laws that are enforced with strict punishments
questions.explanation: Daoism, associated with the book known as the Daodejing, encourages simplicity, humility and going with the flow of nature rather than forcing things. Harsh laws and punishments were the Legalist approach, and rituals and family duties are central to Confucianism. Daoism also influenced Chinese medicine, art and religion.

questions.stem: Which philosophy did the Qin state use to govern, and what did it stress?
options: Legalism, stressing strict laws and harsh punishments
Confucianism, stressing virtue and duty to one's family
Daoism, stressing harmony with the natural world
Buddhism, stressing escape from the cycle of rebirth
questions.explanation: Legalist thinkers such as Han Feizi and the Qin minister Shang Yang argued that people are best controlled by clear laws, rewards and severe punishments applied to everyone, which helped Qin build a powerful state. The Han dynasty later made Confucianism the official philosophy. Buddhism did not reach China until the Han period.

questions.stem: In 221 BCE the ruler of Qin conquered the other states and unified China. What title did he take?
options: Gaozu, founder of the Han dynasty
Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of Qin
Wudi, the Martial Emperor of the Han
Yu the Great, founder of the Xia dynasty
questions.explanation: King Zheng of Qin called himself Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor', expecting his family to rule for ten thousand generations; instead the Qin dynasty collapsed in 206 BCE, soon after his death. The Han dynasty that followed was founded by Liu Bang, later known as Gaozu, and Wudi was a later Han emperor. Yu the Great is a figure of legend.

questions.stem: Which of these was one of Qin Shi Huang's reforms to unify China?
options: Standard writing, coins, weights and cart-axle widths
Exams on the Confucian classics to choose all officials
Making Buddhism the official religion of the empire
Letting each former state keep its own currency
questions.explanation: Qin Shi Huang made the whole empire use one script, one currency, one set of weights and measures and even one axle width, so carts could run in the same ruts on new roads. These reforms helped hold China together long after his dynasty fell. Exams based on Confucian learning developed under the Han and later dynasties.

questions.stem: Qin Shi Huang ordered the burning of many books in 213 BCE. What was the main reason?
options: To silence scholars who used old texts to criticise his rule
Paper was so scarce that old books had to be collected and recycled
A flood had damaged the libraries and the wet books spread disease
To make room in the libraries for new Legalist law codes
questions.explanation: Advised by his minister Li Si, the emperor ordered the burning of histories and Confucian writings that scholars used to praise past rulers and criticise his own, though books on medicine, farming and divination were spared. Later Confucian historians remembered this harshly. Books were then written mainly on bamboo strips, as paper was not yet in common use.

questions.stem: The Terracotta Army, discovered by farmers near Xi'an in 1974, was made to:
options: train real soldiers in battle formations
stand along the top of the Great Wall
guard Qin Shi Huang in the afterlife
defend the capital against northern raiders
questions.explanation: Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, each with individual features, along with horses, chariots and real weapons, were buried in pits near the emperor's tomb to protect him after death. The main tomb mound itself has never been opened. The site is World Heritage listed and is a major source of evidence about the Qin army.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Great Wall of China is accurate?
options: It was built mainly to keep Japanese invaders out of northern China
Qin Shi Huang linked earlier walls, but most of what stands today is Ming
Qin Shi Huang built the whole wall at once, and it has barely changed since
It is easy to see with the naked eye from the surface of the Moon
questions.explanation: Qin Shi Huang joined and extended earlier state walls to defend against northern peoples such as the Xiongnu, and later dynasties rebuilt it many times; the famous brick and stone sections near Beijing were mostly built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). The idea that it can be seen from the Moon is a myth, since the wall is long but very narrow.

questions.stem: The Han dynasty began choosing some officials through recommendation and examination. What were candidates expected to know?
options: The Confucian classics
Legalist law codes only
Buddhist scriptures
Archery and chariot driving
questions.explanation: Emperor Wu made Confucianism the official learning of the state and founded an Imperial Academy to teach the classics, so officials were increasingly chosen for education and good character rather than only family connections. The full imperial examination system developed later, under the Sui and Tang dynasties. Buddhism had barely reached China at this time.

questions.stem: Which invention is traditionally credited to Cai Lun, an official at the Han court, around 105 CE?
options: Paper money
Paper
Gunpowder
Movable type printing
questions.explanation: Cai Lun reported an improved way of making paper from tree bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets, though archaeologists have found earlier paper from the Han period. Paper was cheaper than silk and lighter than bamboo strips, helping spread learning and government records. Gunpowder, movable type and paper money all came centuries later.

questions.stem: Zhang Qian's journeys to Central Asia for Emperor Wu of Han, beginning in 138 BCE, are significant because they:
options: conquered the Roman Empire's eastern provinces for the Han
brought the very first Buddhist monks from India to China
found a sea route from China to the islands of Japan
opened contacts that grew into the Silk Road trade routes
questions.explanation: Zhang Qian was sent west to seek allies against the Xiongnu; he was held captive for about ten years, but his reports on Central Asian kingdoms, horses and goods led the Han to expand west and open trade. Silk, and later paper and ideas, travelled west, while horses, grapes and eventually Buddhism came east. Han China and Rome knew of each other only indirectly.

questions.stem: In Chinese myth, Pangu is the figure who:
options: separated heaven and earth, and whose body became the world
shaped the first human beings out of yellow clay
tamed the great floods by digging channels to the sea
taught people how to farm and use herbs as medicine
questions.explanation: In the Pangu myth, he grew between heaven and earth, pushing them apart, and when he died his breath became the wind, his eyes the sun and moon and his body the mountains and rivers. Nuwa shaped humans from clay, Yu the Great controlled the floods, and Shennong taught farming and medicine. The Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, was honoured as a legendary ancestor of the Chinese people.

questions.stem: Yu the Great, legendary founder of the Xia dynasty, was celebrated for controlling floods. How did the story say he succeeded?
options: He dug channels to lead the water away, where his father's dams had failed
He built a huge dam across the Yellow River, just as his father had done
He prayed to Pangu, who drank up all the floodwaters in a single night
He moved all of the people up into the mountains until the floods had gone
questions.explanation: In the legend, Yu's father Gun tried to block the floods with dams and failed; Yu spent thirteen years dredging channels to guide the water to the sea, and was so dedicated that he passed his own home without going in. His success earned him the throne. Stories like this linked good rulers with controlling China's rivers.

questions.stem: In Confucian ideals of family life in ancient China, a woman was expected to obey:
options: the emperor's local officials rather than her own family
her own mother for her whole life, even after her marriage
her father, then her husband, and then her son as a widow
the village council of elders on all family matters
questions.explanation: The 'three obediences' expected a woman to follow her father before marriage, her husband during marriage and her son if widowed, and she usually moved into her husband's family home. Women ran households, raised children and produced cloth, and some, such as the Han historian Ban Zhao, became highly educated. Real life did not always match the ideal, and women's influence could be considerable.

questions.stem: The Dujiangyan irrigation system, built in Sichuan around 256 BCE, is remarkable because it:
options: supplied water to the pits of the Terracotta Army
still controls floods and irrigates farmland today
was the first canal to link the Yellow River and Yangtze
used steam-powered pumps to lift water onto the fields
questions.explanation: Built under the Qin official Li Bing, Dujiangyan splits the Min River with an artificial levee and channels water onto the Chengdu Plain without a dam, making the region one of China's richest farming areas. It is still in use more than 2,200 years later and is World Heritage listed. The canal linking the Yellow River and the Yangtze was the much later Grand Canal.

questions.stem: Han tombs at Mawangdui held silk paintings, texts, food and the well-preserved body of a noblewoman, Lady Dai. What can tombs like these best tell historians about?
options: The exact population of the whole Han empire
What lies inside Qin Shi Huang's sealed tomb
How the Han elite lived and imagined the afterlife
How ordinary farming families lived and worked each day
questions.explanation: Lady Dai was the wife of a high official, so her tomb's lacquerware, silk clothing, food and painted silk banner showing the journey to the afterlife reveal the life and beliefs of the wealthy. Ordinary people were buried far more simply, so evidence about them is scarcer. This is a common limit of rich burial evidence in any ancient society.
